text:
Shown prices are MSRP and for the most part they have been fake on both sides, regardless if they raised them over msrp or their partners/retailers did. It is kind of a stupid situation we have here. Prices fluctuate quite a bit so you can't really take current price as they depend on the region/day, so everyone calculates "value" with msrp which is fake and is no better than price right now. Best way to fix it in my opinion would be to find a few popular stores, track prices of in-stock GPUs daily and value should be calculated based on "average" price across some period of time(for cheapest available model). 
For example even in US 9070XT at launch(lets say first week) had close to msrp(lets say ~$650) prices and then they went wild and went over $900. It is stupid to take MSRP and calculate value that way, but taking average price for last 30 days seems fair. If they were selling for 650 for 1 week, then for 900 for 3 weeks after that actual value  should be calculated by averaging price over 4 weeks(~$840).
Like at the moment if you ignore Microcenter 9070 XT is at $800 and 5070 Ti is at $840. Amazing price/performance on paper, but absolute clusterfu*k in reality and it all heavily depends on region.

Each memory chip takes 32 bits of the memory bus, thus a 128 bit card can have 4 chips, a 192 bit card can have 6 chips, for now GDDR7 maxes out at 2GB per chips, thus a 128 bit card can have 4x 2GB = 8GB and a 192 bit card can have 6x 2GB = 12GB.

Then you have "clam shelling" meaning you put VRAM chips on both the front and the back of the PCB, which is expensive and generally not a good design, but they need to use it to get more VRAM out of 128 bit cards.
Soon we will have 3GB GDDR7 chips, so expect the super cards to have 50% more memory.
